title: Rank each topic's leak risk first
statement: Before planning lessons or items, rank topics and stories by how much readers and models already know, key nothing to that knowledge, and test the best-known without the text.
example: A probe found 6 of 6 sampled two-part evidence items answerable without the passage, explorer items among them answered from prior knowledge.
detail: A grade-4 red-team review pulled 6 random two-part evidence items, hid the passage and answered all 6, some from prior knowledge of the real-world facts the course teaches, although the course's rubric gate had passed all six. The course's topic plan then ranked each unit's prior-knowledge risk, highest for its best-known exploration and colonial topics, and set a design consequence for each level: items anchored to the passage's own particulars, and a mandatory cross-family text-hidden check before any item ships. Its topic rubric puts a ceiling on how much a topic's allusion density counts for the same reason: knowledge that saturates children's media and model training makes items answerable without the passage. In a grade-5 assessment, 28 of 36 evaluable items leaked, traced to passages built on widely known domain facts.
against: Prior knowledge was not the only cause in that probe: evidence options restating the first part's answer, and distractor tells, also let items leak (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g4-reading/approval-package/RED_TEAM_FINDINGS.md`, lines 33-35). No measurement shows leaks rising steadily with how well known a topic is. The research note calls its case against the best-known takeaway an argument, not a finding (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l2-the-cyclops.md`, line 442); the lesson plan accepts it on its merits.

evidence.quote: The G4 red team proved the trap empirically: **6/6 sampled EBSR items were blind-solvable, including Magellan/explorer items answerable from prior knowledge.** Knowledge-rich topics make this *worse*, the better we teach world knowledge, the more items become answerable without the passage unless disjointness is designed in.
Items anchor to passage-specific particulars (this voyage's dates/decisions/quotes), never to canon facts; cross-family blind-solve gate mandatory before any item ships

Extremely high allusion density means the knowledge saturates children's media and LLM pretraining — so assessment items over it become answerable *without the passage* (the measured Magellan failure).
I pulled **6 random EBSR items** live, stripped the passage, and attempted them blind. **6/6 were solvable without the passage:**
the knowledge-expedition design makes items about real-world facts (pitch physics, Magellan, explorer funding) answerable by any knowledgeable solver with no passage.
The rubric gate (item ≥0.85 + lesson-level >20% rule) **passed all six of these items** — so the rubric is demonstrably not a substitute for the empirical run.
Sequence / match / EBSR (36 evaluable items): **8 cold (22%), 28 leaked (78%)**
Passages rely on widely-known domain facts; a language model can answer items from prior knowledge alone.

First, it is blind-solvable. "Odysseus is clever" is the single most widely known fact about Odysseus, it is the answer Storyworks prints in its own key, and a child who has never read our passage will produce it. A SPINE lesson whose target concept can be stated correctly without reading fails R-Q-3 at the level of the lesson rather than the item.

Against: it is blind-solvable, since Odysseus is clever is the single most widely known fact about him and a child who has never read our passage will produce it, which fails R-Q-3 at the level of the lesson rather than the item
It cannot catch a question whose answer a child already holds.
The film is rated R, so most nine year olds will not have seen it, but trailers, posters and playground talk are not rated.
What this makes unusable. Any item whose answer is a plot fact about either episode: - What did Circe do to the men. Answer available verbatim from a television episode broadcast this year.

So the design rule follows from the risk: no item's correct answer may be a plot fact. Every answer must be a motive, a clue selection, or a category judgement, and every option must be quotable from our passage
